If you're truly on a track to become an executive someday or found your own company and make it successful, you will find that the compensation is so much backloaded that you would make 90% of your compensation in the last five years of your career, so optimizing for 10%, 20% early in your career.

answer.summary: Choose a place where you can recruit people and genuinely help them build their careers, and check that you’ll have a strong engineering partner and clear alignment on how you’ll work together.

sections.heading: Choose a place that helps people grow
sections.content: Yehoshua advises managers to go somewhere they can recruit. A useful test is whether hiring there would make candidates’ careers: will they learn and grow, and can you earnestly tell them they can build a career there? She raised this in the context of considering turnaround jobs, while noting that turning one around could still be a reason to take it.

sections.heading: Evaluate your working partnership
sections.content: Before joining, make sure you have a good engineering partner who can help get ideas built. Also clarify roles and responsibilities, where you’ll divide and conquer, and where you need to stay aligned; conflicting opinions from the two partners can create organizational confusion.

judgment.explanation: The answer’s advice to choose a place where hires can learn, grow, and advance is supported by S2. The engineering-partner and alignment advice is supported by S3, though it is less relevant to the question. The answer omits Yehoshua’s advice to prioritize learning lasting skills and not rely on predicting financial success or choosing a top brand, so it does not cover all reference points. It makes no claim that those details are unavailable.
